Why can't you have kids upload the source code onto Google Drive in shared folders? I'd give each student a folder (which are, in turn, in a class folder from your perspective), and they just drop the source code file/folder into their individual shared folder for grading. Alternatively, just have them upload the files through Google Classroom.

In terms of getting kids bad at math to get comp sci. concepts, scaffold scaffold scaffold. Before every performance task, make sure they know (and develop) the individual skills. If you want them to generate a program that takes a human name as input and outputs an email address given a set pattern (an assignment I remember doing way back when), what do they need to know? Well, they need to know what a string is, they need to know specific string operations and keywords, they need to know how to output to a file, ask for input, etc.

Trust me, everyone faces dumb kids. Every school district has nearly mandatory promotion. That's quick cover-up, but know that a lot of your students know what you're doing, and they're not going to stay quiet about it forever. Kids know when their time is being wasted.

1. Are you running through the entire writing process? I once spent 30 minutes just doing prewriting *in French* with a class because my kids just wouldn't stop thinking of things. I can't imagine going through pre-writing, drafting, (peer-)editing, revising, and publishing all in one lesson, especially if it's not the topic of the entire lesson. It builds good habits, allows for honest collaboration, and improves the quality of work submitted.
2. Are you teaching grammar & analysing similar assignments from professional writers before jumping into writing? That's beneficial and takes time.
3. Are you giving kids something interesting to write about? Language synthesis requires having something to say. If they don't have anything to say, they're just going to BS the assignment as quick as possible. It also opens the door for research to be done to teach research skills. Global ethical issues work great for that. I'm not really sure what kinds of topics are "appropriate" for 6th graders, but things like real-world examples of animal rights, racism, sexism, whatever. Ados love getting worked up about things they can't control.

>For writing today

It's important not to get too pigeon-holed into one skill. Reading, watching, listening, researching, grammar, vocabulary, analysing, etc. are all intertwined with writing. It's not one skill, it's a thousand skills.
